voiceover: Cleopatra lived closer to us than to the pyramids.
visual: Ancient coin portrait of Cleopatra, museum open-access photo

voiceover: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC.
visual: Timeline graphic: pyramid icon at 2560 BC

voiceover: That gap is roughly 2,500 years. To her, the pyramids were already ancient monuments.
Now count forward. From Cleopatra to the Moon landing in 1969 is about 2,000 years.
visual: Timeline extends to a rocket icon at 1969

voiceover: Egypt’s history is that deep. Which other timeline should I line up next?
visual: Full timeline, three icons, slow zoom out

voiceover: Medieval people did not think the Earth was flat.
visual: Medieval round-world map (public domain); flat map crossed out

voiceover: Scholars like the English monk Bede, around 700, wrote about a round Earth.
Medieval kings even held a ball with a cross, a symbol of rule over the world.
The flat-Earth story mostly spread in the 1800s, in popular books about Columbus.
So the myth is newer than the people it describes. What myth should I check next?
Magellan never actually sailed around the world.
visual: Old map of Magellan’s route (public domain)

voiceover: Five ships left Spain in 1519, led by Ferdinand Magellan, heading west.
visual: Map: five ship icons leave Spain

voiceover: In 1521 Magellan was killed in a fight in the Philippines, partway through the trip.
Juan Sebastián Elcano took over. In 1522 one ship, the Victoria, reached Spain again.
visual: Map: one ship completes the loop

voiceover: About eighteen men made it home. Who do you think deserves the credit?
This blurry rooftop view took hours to photograph.
visual: Museum open-access image of the Niépce heliograph

voiceover: Around 1826, Nicéphore Niépce pointed a camera out of a window in France.
visual: Simple re-creation: window, camera box sketch

voiceover: He used a plate coated with bitumen that hardened slowly in sunlight.
visual: Diagram: light hits a coated plate

voiceover: The exposure probably took many hours, maybe days. It’s the oldest surviving camera photograph.
Today that takes a split second. What would you photograph if you had one shot?
visual: Phone camera icon beside the heliograph

voiceover: Russian men once paid a tax to keep beards.
visual: Artefact photo: bronze beard tax token

voiceover: In 1698, Tsar Peter the Great wanted Russia to look more like western Europe.
visual: Period portrait of Peter I (public domain)

voiceover: Beards were out. Men who kept one could pay a tax and carry a token as proof.
visual: Re-creation: token passed hand to hand

voiceover: Prices reportedly varied by rank, with wealthy merchants paying far more than others.
visual: Simple chart: rank vs price, no numbers

voiceover: Would you pay to keep your beard, or shave it?
In 1666, a small bakery fire swallowed London.
visual: Period painting of the Great Fire (public domain)

voiceover: It began early on September 2 in Thomas Farriner’s bakery on Pudding Lane.
visual: Old London street map, pin on Pudding Lane

voiceover: Strong winds and wooden houses let it spread for about four days.
Around 13,000 houses burned. Only a few deaths were recorded, but the true number is unknown.
London rebuilt in brick and stone. Should I cover how they rebuilt it?
Medieval people drank water too. Here’s the real story.
visual: Period painting of a village well (public domain)

voiceover: The popular version says water was so dirty that everyone drank beer all day.
visual: Re-creation: beer mugs, red question mark

voiceover: Written sources mention wells, springs and water carriers. People knew which sources were clean.
visual: Manuscript illustration of a water carrier

voiceover: Weak ale, often called small beer, was common too. It was cheap calories as much as a drink.
visual: Simple re-creation: bread loaf beside ale

voiceover: So both are true, just not the myth. What other food fact should I check?
An entire English colony vanished, leaving one carved word.
visual: Old engraving of Roanoke Island (public domain)

voiceover: In 1587, about 115 settlers arrived on Roanoke Island, in today’s North Carolina.
Their governor, John White, sailed to England for supplies. War delayed his return for three years.
visual: Map: ship icon crosses Atlantic and back

voiceover: In 1590 the houses were gone. ‘CROATOAN’ was carved on a post, the name of a nearby island.
What happened to them is still debated. What do you think happened?
visual: Slow zoom on the carved word

voiceover: Ancient Rome taxed urine. And laundries wanted it.
visual: Ancient wall painting of a laundry (public domain)

voiceover: Roman cloth workers, called fullers, used urine to clean and soften wool clothes.
The ammonia in it helped lift dirt and grease. Jars were collected from public places.
visual: Simple diagram: jar on a street corner

voiceover: Emperor Vespasian placed a tax on this trade, so even waste brought money in.
visual: Ancient coin of Vespasian, museum open-access photo

voiceover: Weird, but it worked. Which ancient job would you refuse to do?
The Bayeux Tapestry isn’t really a tapestry.
visual: Public-domain photo of the Bayeux embroidery

voiceover: A tapestry is woven on a loom. This one is embroidered: wool stitched onto linen.
It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England in 1066, scene by scene.
It is about 70 metres long and was probably made within a few years of 1066.
Same story, wrong name. Which famous object has a misleading name?
Ships got lost because no clock worked at sea.
Sailors could find latitude from the sun, but longitude needed exact time.
Pendulum clocks failed on rolling ships. Britain offered a large prize in 1714 for a solution.
Carpenter turned clockmaker John Harrison built several sea clocks. His watch H4 passed a voyage test.
A pocket watch solved it. What invention do you think saved more sailors?
Lightning never struck Ben Franklin’s kite.
visual: Period painting of Franklin’s kite (public domain)

voiceover: Franklin described flying a kite in a storm in 1752, with a metal key tied on.
Electric charge from the storm clouds collected on the wet string and the key. He felt sparks.
visual: Diagram: charge travels down the string

voiceover: A direct strike would likely have killed him. The point was to show lightning is electricity.
It led to the lightning rod. Which experiment would you want to watch live?
In Tudor England, purple silk was off-limits to most.
visual: Tudor portrait in rich fabric (public domain)

voiceover: Laws called statutes of apparel set what each rank was allowed to wear.
visual: Re-creation: ranking ladder with fabric icons

voiceover: Purple silk was for the royal family. Some furs, velvets and gold cloth needed high rank.
The goal was to keep social ranks visible at a glance, and to limit spending on imports.
visual: Simple graphic: crowd sorted by color

voiceover: Clothes showed your place. Which of your clothes would the Tudors ban?
On November 9, 1989, a wall opened overnight.
Since 1961, the Berlin Wall had split the city into East and West.
That evening, a confused announcement suggested new travel rules started immediately.
Crowds gathered at the crossings, and the guards opened the gates. Demolition came later, in 1990.
One night changed a city. Which turning-point day should I tell next?
Before alarm clocks, people paid someone to wake them.
visual: Re-creation silhouette: figure with a long pole

voiceover: In industrial British towns, mill and factory shifts started early, before sunrise.
visual: Period painting of a mill town (public domain)

voiceover: A knocker-upper walked the streets with a long pole and tapped on upstairs windows.
They stayed until someone answered, then moved to the next house on the list.
The job faded as alarm clocks got cheaper. How do you make sure you wake up?
The Library of Alexandria didn’t vanish in one fire.
visual: Old engraving of the library (public domain)

voiceover: The popular version says one huge blaze wiped out the ancient world’s knowledge.
visual: Re-creation: scrolls in flames, red question mark

voiceover: A fire around 48 BC may have damaged part of the collection. The library continued afterward.
Over centuries it lost funding, scholars and protection, and slowly declined.
visual: Timeline graphic: slow fade to grey

voiceover: A slow fade, not one fire. Which lost book would you bring back?
You can’t see the Great Wall from the Moon.
visual: Photo of the Great Wall, open-licence

voiceover: The wall is very long, but most sections are only a few metres wide.
From the Moon, about 384,000 kilometres away, that is like spotting a hair from kilometres off.
visual: Simple graphic: Earth from the Moon

voiceover: Astronauts in low orbit have said it is very hard to spot without help.
Huge, but thin. What other space myth have you heard?
This cathedral took over six hundred years to finish.
Work on Cologne Cathedral in Germany started in 1248, in the Gothic style.
Around the 1470s, building stopped. A medieval crane stayed on the unfinished tower for centuries.
visual: Old engraving of the crane on the tower (public domain)

voiceover: In the 1800s, workers used the original medieval plans to complete it. It was finished in 1880.
Six centuries for one building. What took you the longest to finish?
Vikings reached North America almost 500 years before Columbus.
visual: Map: North Atlantic route, Greenland to Newfoundland

voiceover: Old Norse sagas described a land called Vinland, west of Greenland.
In the 1960s, archaeologists dug at L’Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, Canada.
They found Norse-style buildings and objects from around the year 1000. The stay was short.
visual: Photo of rebuilt turf houses, open-licence

voiceover: So Columbus wasn’t first. Which history ‘first’ do you think is wrong?
The first computer program was written in 1843.
visual: Period portrait of Ada Lovelace (public domain)

voiceover: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculator that was never finished.
visual: Museum photo of Babbage’s engine parts, open-access

voiceover: Ada Lovelace translated an article about it and added notes longer than the article itself.
visual: Re-creation: two paper stacks, hers taller

voiceover: One note set out steps for the machine to calculate a sequence of numbers.
She also guessed machines could do more than math. Who should I cover next?
European courts once put pigs on trial. Really.
visual: Medieval manuscript image of a courtroom (public domain)

voiceover: From roughly the 1300s to the 1700s, records describe animals charged in courts across Europe.
visual: Map of Europe with case pins

voiceover: Pigs were common defendants, usually for causing harm on farms. Some cases had a formal hearing and a verdict.
visual: Re-creation: pig silhouette in a dock

voiceover: Church courts handled pests too. Rats and insects that ate crops were sometimes formally warned to leave.
visual: Manuscript margin drawing of insects (public domain)

voiceover: Historians link these trials to ideas about order and justice: even harm by an animal needed a public answer.
A collection of cases was published in 1906. Which animal would you put on trial today?
The first powered flight lasted only twelve seconds.
visual: Public-domain photo of the 1903 Wright Flyer

voiceover: On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright tested their engine-powered Flyer near Kitty Hawk.
visual: Map pin on Kitty Hawk, North Carolina

voiceover: Orville flew first. The plane covered about 120 feet, less than the wingspan of a large jet.
They flew four times that day. The longest flight, by Wilbur, lasted about 59 seconds.
A gust of wind then damaged the plane, and it never flew again. It is now in a museum.
visual: Museum photo of the Flyer, open-access

voiceover: Sixty-six years later, people walked on the Moon. What invention do you think moved fastest?
Ice from frozen ponds once sailed to the tropics.
visual: Period engraving of ice harvesting (public domain)

voiceover: In 1806, a Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor shipped ice to the Caribbean. People laughed at him.
Workers sawed blocks from frozen ponds in winter and packed them in sawdust to slow the melting.
visual: Re-creation: ice blocks stacked in sawdust

voiceover: Tudor built insulated ice houses at the ports. Over the years his ice trade became profitable.
By the 1830s, ships even carried New England ice to India, a voyage of several months.
visual: Map: route around Africa to India

voiceover: Ice was once a luxury import. Which everyday item do you think was once a luxury?
Six centuries old, and nobody can read this book.
visual: Public-domain scan of a Voynich manuscript page

voiceover: It is called the Voynich manuscript, after a book dealer who bought it in 1912.
Its vellum pages were radiocarbon dated to the early 1400s. They hold about 240 pages of unknown script.
There are drawings of plants nobody has identified, star charts and bathing figures. Some pages fold out.
visual: Slow pan over drawings (public domain scans)

voiceover: Professional code-breakers and many researchers have tried. No proposed reading has been widely accepted.
It sits at Yale today. Is it a code, a lost language, or a hoax?
The pyramids weren’t built by slaves. Here’s the evidence.
visual: Photo of the Giza pyramids, open-licence

voiceover: The popular version shows whipped slaves dragging stones. It spread through old histories and films.
visual: Re-creation: red question mark over the scene

voiceover: Archaeologists found a workers’ town near Giza, with bakeries, sleeping halls and many animal bones from food.
visual: Map: workers’ town beside the pyramids

voiceover: They also found workers’ tombs close to the pyramids. Enslaved people would not usually get such burials.
The likely picture is skilled crews plus rotating labourers called up for a season, paid partly in food.
Hard work, but not slavery as shown in films. What ancient myth should I check next?
Medieval people didn’t all die at thirty. Averages mislead.
visual: Medieval painting of elderly villagers (public domain)

voiceover: You may have heard that medieval life expectancy was around 30, so adults died young.
visual: Re-creation: number 30 with red question mark

voiceover: But an average includes babies and children. Many children died very young, which pulls the average far down.
visual: Simple chart: ages spread, average line drops

voiceover: If you survived childhood, your chances changed. Many adults lived into their fifties or sixties, some much longer.
So 30 was the average at birth, not a typical age of death for grown adults.
One number, two meanings. What history statistic confused you as a kid?
Decades before Columbus, Chinese fleets reached East Africa.
visual: Old map of the Indian Ocean (public domain)

voiceover: Between 1405 and 1433, the admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages for the Ming emperors.
The fleets were huge. The first reportedly carried around 27,000 people on many ships.
visual: Simple graphic: fleet of ship icons

voiceover: They sailed to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and the coast of East Africa, trading and showing Ming power.
visual: Map: routes across the Indian Ocean

voiceover: The exact size of the biggest ships is debated. Some accounts may exaggerate them.
visual: Re-creation: ship outline with question mark

voiceover: After 1433 the voyages stopped, and the fleets were never sent again. Why do you think China ended them?
In 1844, a message crossed forty miles almost instantly.
visual: Public-domain photo of a Morse telegraph key

voiceover: Before that, news traveled as fast as a horse, a train or a ship could carry it.
visual: Re-creation: horse, train and ship icons

voiceover: Samuel Morse and his partners built a telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore, about 40 miles.
visual: Map: line between the two cities

voiceover: On May 24, 1844, Morse tapped out a Bible phrase: what hath God wrought. It arrived in Baltimore.
visual: Paper tape graphic with dots and dashes

voiceover: Within a few decades, telegraph wires crossed continents and, from 1866, the Atlantic Ocean.
Words at the speed of electricity. What would your first message be?
Britain once taxed people for their windows.
visual: Photo of a bricked-up window, own photo or open-licence

voiceover: In 1696, England introduced a window tax. Houses with more windows paid more.
The idea was simple. Windows could be counted from the street, so officials didn’t need to go inside.
Many owners bricked up windows to pay less. You can still see blocked windows on some old buildings.
Critics said it cut light and fresh air in crowded homes. The tax was finally abolished in 1851.
It lasted 155 years. Have you ever spotted a bricked-up window near you?
visual: Slow zoom on the blocked window

voiceover: In 1752, Britain skipped eleven days in one night.
visual: Re-creation: calendar page, Sept 3–13 crossed out

voiceover: The old Julian calendar ran a little long, so it slowly drifted away from the seasons.
Catholic countries had switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1582. Britain waited about 170 years.
To catch up, Wednesday, September 2, 1752 was followed by Thursday, September 14. The days between never happened.
There’s a famous story about riots demanding the lost days back. Evidence for real riots is thin.
visual: Re-creation: crowd with red question mark

voiceover: The same change reached the American colonies. Which day would you happily skip?
Kitchens once used small dogs to turn the roast.
visual: Period illustration of a turnspit wheel (public domain)

voiceover: Meat was roasted on a spit in front of the fire, and it had to keep turning.
visual: Re-creation: spit in front of a fireplace

voiceover: In many British kitchens, a small breed called the turnspit dog ran inside a wooden wheel on the wall.
visual: Diagram: wheel linked to spit by a belt

voiceover: The wheel was linked to the spit, so as the dog ran, the meat turned. Shifts could be long.
visual: Simple animation: wheel turns, spit turns

voiceover: Mechanical spits replaced them in the 1800s, and the breed died out. A preserved one is in a Welsh museum.
A whole breed gone with one job. Which old job should I explain next?
Amelia Earhart vanished in 1937. Nobody found her plane.
visual: Public-domain photo of Earhart’s Lockheed Electra

voiceover: Earhart was famous already. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
In 1937, she and navigator Fred Noonan set out to fly around the world near the equator.
On July 2, they left New Guinea for Howland Island, a tiny speck in the Pacific. They never arrived.
visual: Map: route ends before Howland Island

voiceover: A huge search found nothing. Theories include running out of fuel at sea or landing on another island.
visual: Re-creation: search ships on a map

voiceover: None has been proven. What do you think happened on that last flight?
visual: Slow zoom on the empty ocean

voiceover: This Roman dome has stood for nearly 1,900 years.
visual: Public-domain photo of the Pantheon dome interior

voiceover: The Pantheon in Rome was rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian around AD 125, and it is still in use.
Its dome is about 43 metres across. It has no steel inside: it is unreinforced concrete.
The builders made the concrete lighter toward the top, using lighter stone mixed in, and thinner walls.
visual: Diagram: heavy at base, light at top

voiceover: At the very top is an open hole, the oculus, about nine metres wide. Rain falls straight in.
visual: Photo looking up at the oculus

voiceover: Still the largest dome of its kind. Which ancient building would you visit first?
One workshop in Mainz changed how Europe made books.
visual: Public-domain scan of a Gutenberg Bible page

voiceover: Before the 1450s, almost every book in Europe was copied by hand, often taking months.
visual: Manuscript illustration of a scribe (public domain)

voiceover: Johannes Gutenberg developed a system of movable metal type, oil-based ink and a press adapted from wine presses.
Around 1455 his workshop finished a large Latin Bible. Historians estimate about 180 copies were printed.
Gutenberg lost his workshop to his financial partner after a lawsuit. Printing spread across Europe anyway.
visual: Map: printing spreads city by city

voiceover: Fewer than 50 copies survive today. Which book would you have printed first?
On long voyages, sailors feared scurvy more than storms.
visual: Period painting of a sailing warship (public domain)

voiceover: Scurvy caused weakness and bleeding gums on long voyages. We now know it comes from lacking vitamin C.
visual: Re-creation: ship’s biscuit and salt meat

voiceover: In 1747, ship’s surgeon James Lind tested treatments on twelve sick sailors, in pairs.
The pair given oranges and lemons improved fastest. It was one of the earliest controlled trials in medicine.
But the Navy didn’t act at once. Lemon juice became a routine ration only around 1795.
Nearly fifty years for a fix. Which good idea do you think took too long?
In 1895, a glowing screen led to the X-ray.
visual: Public-domain X-ray image of a hand with a ring

voiceover: On November 8, Wilhelm Röntgen was testing a covered electric tube in his German lab.
visual: Re-creation: lab bench with a glass tube

voiceover: A coated screen across the room started to glow, even though the tube was covered.
visual: Diagram: invisible rays reach a screen

voiceover: He called the unknown rays X-rays. Weeks later he made an image of his wife’s hand, showing bones and a ring.
visual: Slow zoom on the hand image

voiceover: Doctors began using X-rays within months. In 1901 Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
An accident changed medicine. Which accidental discovery surprises you most?
English kings banned football again and again.
visual: Medieval manuscript drawing of a ball game (public domain)

voiceover: Medieval football wasn’t a tidy match. Crowds chased a ball through streets, with few rules.
visual: Re-creation: crowd silhouettes and a ball

voiceover: In 1314, a proclamation in London banned it, worried about noise and disorder in the city.
Later, Edward III wanted men practising archery for war instead of playing ball games.
Similar bans were repeated for centuries, in England and in Scotland, which suggests people kept playing anyway.
Football outlasted every single ban, and today it fills stadiums. Which modern sport would annoy a medieval king most?
One golden spike finished a railroad across America.
Two companies built toward each other, one from California and one from the Midwest.
visual: Map: two lines approaching each other

voiceover: Thousands of workers, many from China and Ireland, laid the track across mountains and plains.
visual: Period photo of track workers (public domain)

voiceover: On May 10, 1869, the lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah. A telegraph sent one word: done.
The golden spike was removed right after the ceremony. It is kept at a Stanford museum today.
visual: Museum photo of the spike, open-access

voiceover: A trip of weeks or months became about a week. Which turning-point day should I cover next?
Ancient Romans had street food counters, like fast food.
visual: Public-domain photo of a Pompeii food counter

voiceover: In Pompeii, archaeologists have found many counters called thermopolia along the streets.
visual: Map of Pompeii with counter pins

voiceover: Each had a masonry counter with large jars set into the top, for hot or dry food.
Many city flats had no proper kitchen, so buying food outside was part of everyday life.
visual: Re-creation: small flat without a kitchen

voiceover: Some counters were painted with animals and scenes. Remains in jars suggest dishes with meat, fish and beans.
visual: Close-up of a painted counter, open-licence

voiceover: Lunch on the go, about 2,000 years ago. What would you order in Pompeii?
In 1872, a ship was found drifting, nobody aboard.
visual: Public-domain painting of the Mary Celeste

voiceover: The Mary Celeste had left New York for Genoa, carrying barrels of industrial alcohol.
visual: Map: New York to Genoa route

voiceover: A month later, another ship found her drifting near the Azores. The crew of ten was gone.
Her cargo was mostly intact and there was food on board. Her lifeboat was missing.
visual: Re-creation: empty davits where a boat hung

voiceover: One common theory: fear of a leak or fumes made them leave in the lifeboat, then they were lost.
visual: Diagram: ship and small boat drifting apart

voiceover: Nobody was ever found. What do you think made them leave the ship?
This broken stone let people read hieroglyphs again.
visual: Museum open-access photo of the Rosetta Stone

voiceover: For over a thousand years, nobody could read Egyptian hieroglyphs. The knowledge had been lost.
In 1799, French soldiers in Egypt found a carved slab near the town of Rosetta.
visual: Map pin on Rosetta, Nile Delta

voiceover: It carried one decree from 196 BC, written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic script and in ancient Greek.
Scholars could read the Greek. So they had the same message in a script they knew, beside two they didn’t.
visual: Diagram: Greek band lit, arrows to others

voiceover: Names like Ptolemy sat inside oval frames called cartouches. Matching those names gave the first sound values.
In 1822, Jean-François Champollion announced he could read the system. Egypt’s own words could be read again.
The stone is in the British Museum. Which lost script would you want to read?
Vikings never wore horned helmets into battle.
visual: 1800s painting of a horned warrior (public domain), red X

voiceover: That image is everywhere: cartoons, sports logos, costumes. But archaeologists have never found a Viking-age helmet with horns.
visual: Your own quick doodles of horned helmets

voiceover: The best-preserved one, the Gjermundbu helmet, was found in Norway in 1943. It’s a rounded iron cap with eye guards.
visual: Line drawing of the Gjermundbu helmet

voiceover: No horns. Horns would be a terrible idea in a fight: they give a blade something to catch.
visual: Re-creation: helmet outline, horns fade out

voiceover: So where did the horns come from? Mostly the 1800s. Painters and costume designers gave Norse heroes horns and wings to look dramatic.
A famous example: the first full staging of Wagner’s Ring cycle in 1876, whose costumes gave several characters horned helmets.
Real horned helmets do exist, found in Denmark. But they’re Bronze Age ceremonial pieces, well over a thousand years older than the Viking age.
visual: Map of Denmark, pin drops; timeline zooms out

voiceover: What history fact did you learn as a kid that turned out wrong?
They crossed thousands of miles of ocean without maps.
visual: Map of the Pacific triangle: Hawaii, New Zealand, Rapa Nui

voiceover: Over many centuries, Polynesian navigators settled islands spread across a huge triangle of the Pacific.
visual: Map: arrows spread island to island

voiceover: The last big ones, like Hawaii and New Zealand, were settled roughly 800 to 1,000 years ago.
Navigators read the night sky. They memorized where stars rose and set on the horizon, and steered by them.
By day they felt ocean swells against the hull. Swell patterns bend around islands long before land appears.
visual: Diagram: swells bending around an island

voiceover: Birds helped too. Some seabirds fly out to fish in the morning and return to land at dusk.
visual: Simple graphic: bird flight lines toward an island

voiceover: Some once argued these islands were found by accident. Planned voyages explain the evidence better.
Stars, waves and birds. Which clue would you trust most on open water?
visual: Starry sky over ocean, slow zoom

voiceover: Galileo didn’t invent the telescope. Here’s who did.
visual: Public-domain drawing of an early telescope

voiceover: In 1608, Dutch spectacle maker Hans Lipperhey sought a patent for a device making distant things look closer.
He wasn’t the only one. Other Dutch makers claimed it too, so the patent was not granted.
News spread fast. In 1609, Galileo Galilei in Italy heard about it and built his own, much stronger version.
Then he did what made him famous: he pointed it at the sky and wrote down what he saw.
visual: Museum photo of Galileo’s telescope, open-access

voiceover: He saw mountains on the Moon and, in 1610, four moons circling Jupiter.
visual: Simple graphic: Jupiter with four dots

voiceover: So he didn’t invent it. He turned a curiosity into a tool for astronomy.
Which inventor do you think gets credit for someone else’s idea?
Early British vehicles needed a walker carrying a flag.
visual: Re-creation: walker with red flag ahead of a steam vehicle

voiceover: In 1865, Britain passed a Locomotive Act for steam-powered vehicles on public roads.
The speed limit was four miles an hour in the country and two miles an hour in towns.
Each vehicle needed a crew, and one person had to walk in front, warning riders and horses, carrying a red flag.
visual: Diagram: crew positions around the vehicle

voiceover: Lawmakers worried about frightened horses, damaged roads and noisy machines. Horses were still the main traffic.
visual: Period engraving of a busy road (public domain)

voiceover: In 1878 the flag rule was relaxed. Early petrol cars arrived, still under strict rules.
In 1896 a new law raised the limit to 14 miles an hour. Drivers celebrated with a run to Brighton.
Which rule of today will look strange in 100 years?
London smelled so bad in 1858, it built sewers.
visual: Period cartoon of the Thames (public domain)

voiceover: For years, London’s sewage and waste flowed straight into the River Thames, the same river many drew water from.
visual: Map of the Thames through London

voiceover: In the hot summer of 1858, the river’s smell became so strong people called it the Great Stink.
Parliament sat right beside the river. Curtains were reportedly soaked in chemicals to block the smell.
visual: Engraving of the Houses of Parliament (public domain)

voiceover: Lawmakers who had delayed for years suddenly moved quickly and approved a huge sewer plan within weeks.
Engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed it: large brick tunnels that carried waste away from central London.
visual: Diagram: tunnels running beside the river

voiceover: The new system helped end the city’s cholera outbreaks, and parts of it are still in use today.
visual: Photo of a Victorian sewer tunnel, open-licence

voiceover: A bad smell changed a city. What hidden system in your town do you never think about?
This tiny black stamp changed how letters got paid.
visual: Museum open-access image of the Penny Black

voiceover: Before 1840, British letters were usually paid for by the person receiving them, priced by distance and sheets.
That made post expensive and slow to collect. Some people refused letters to avoid paying.
visual: Simple graphic: letter returned to sender

voiceover: A reformer named Rowland Hill proposed one cheap rate, paid in advance by the sender.
In 1840, Britain introduced the uniform penny post. One penny sent a light letter anywhere in the country.
visual: Map of Britain, letters fly in all directions

voiceover: On May 6, 1840, the Penny Black became valid, the world’s first adhesive postage stamp.
Letter numbers rose sharply within a few years, and other countries soon introduced their own stamps.
Today, billions of stamps later, when did you last send a paper letter?
Thousands of these seals survive. Nobody can read them.
visual: Museum open-access photo of an Indus seal

voiceover: The Indus civilization grew along rivers in today’s Pakistan and northwest India, about 4,500 years ago.
visual: Map of the Indus Valley region

voiceover: Its cities, like Mohenjo-daro, had planned streets, brick houses and covered drains.
They also left thousands of small carved seals, often with an animal and a short row of symbols.
The inscriptions are very short, usually just a few signs. That gives code-breakers little to work with.
visual: Simple graphic: five signs in a row

voiceover: There is no known bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone, that pairs this script with a known one.
visual: Re-creation: Rosetta Stone outline, crossed out

voiceover: Many decipherments have been proposed. None is widely accepted, and scholars even debate what language it records.
Which lost script do you think will be cracked next?
This corroded shipwreck lump is full of ancient gears.
visual: Museum open-access photo of the Antikythera fragments

voiceover: In 1901, sponge divers recovered objects from an ancient wreck near the Greek island of Antikythera.
Among statues and pottery were some lumps of corroded bronze. Months later someone noticed a gear wheel.
Scans in modern times revealed dozens of interlocking gears and tiny inscriptions inside the fragments.
It was likely made around the second or first century BC. Dates vary between studies.
Turning a handle moved dials showing the Sun, the Moon and predicted eclipses.
Nothing this complex is known again until the medieval astronomical clocks of Europe, many centuries later.
visual: Timeline graphic: gap to medieval clocks

voiceover: Who built it, and exactly why, is still unknown. Which ancient object would you want to study?
Medieval chess pieces turned up on a Scottish island.
visual: Museum open-access photo of the Lewis chessmen

voiceover: In 1831 a hoard of small carved figures was found on the Isle of Lewis, in Scotland’s Outer Hebrides.
visual: Map pin on the Isle of Lewis

voiceover: There were dozens of chess pieces: kings, queens, bishops, knights and warders, plus game pieces.
visual: Simple graphic: piece types in a row

voiceover: Most are carved from walrus ivory, some from whale teeth. They date to around the late 1100s.
visual: Close-up of the ivory carving, open-access

voiceover: Their style suggests they were probably made in Norway, perhaps in Trondheim, then carried west.
visual: Map: Norway to the Hebrides route

voiceover: How they ended up buried on Lewis is not known. A merchant’s stock is one idea.
visual: Re-creation: small bag buried in sand

voiceover: Some warders bite the tops of their shields, which makes them one of the most loved museum objects.
Which piece would you put on your board?
Ice crushed their ship. Every crew member survived.
visual: Public-domain photo of Endurance in pack ice

voiceover: In 1914, the explorer Ernest Shackleton sailed south, aiming to cross the whole of Antarctica on foot.
visual: Map of Antarctica with planned route

voiceover: In early 1915 his ship, Endurance, was trapped in sea ice. Months later the ice crushed it and it sank.
The 28 men camped on drifting ice, then took three small boats to tiny Elephant Island.
Shackleton and five others sailed a small lifeboat about 800 miles to South Georgia to get help.
visual: Map: Elephant Island to South Georgia

voiceover: Then they crossed the island’s mountains to reach a whaling station. Rescue took several attempts.
In August 1916, a Chilean ship rescued all the men left on Elephant Island.
All of them came home. What quality would you most want in a leader?
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
She was born in Warsaw in 1867 and moved to Paris to study physics and mathematics.
With her husband Pierre, she studied the strange rays given off by uranium and other minerals.
visual: Re-creation: mineral sample and measuring device

voiceover: In 1898 they announced two new elements: polonium, named after Poland, and radium.
In 1903 she shared the Nobel Prize in Physics. She was the first woman to win one.
In 1911 she won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own, for her work on radium and polonium.
Her notebooks are still radioactive today, and readers reportedly handle them with protective precautions.
visual: Re-creation: notebook in a lined box

voiceover: Her story is still taught worldwide. Which scientist do you think deserves more fame?
In 1795, Britain taxed people for powdering their hair.
visual: Period portrait with powdered wig (public domain)

voiceover: Powdered wigs and hair were high fashion in the 1700s. The powder was usually made from starch or flour.
Britain was at war with France, and the government needed money. Food prices were also rising.
Prime Minister William Pitt introduced a duty: anyone using hair powder had to buy a yearly certificate.
visual: Simple graphic: certificate with a seal

voiceover: Some exceptions applied, for example to the royal family and some clergy, and certain servants were covered by employers.
Many people simply stopped powdering. Fashion was already moving toward natural hair, and the tax sped it up.
Few people still paid by the 1800s. The tax was finally repealed in 1869.
Which fashion would you happily see taxed?
In 1957, a metal ball started beeping from orbit.
The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first human-made object to orbit Earth.
visual: Simple graphic: Earth with an orbit line

voiceover: It was a polished sphere about 58 centimetres wide, with four long antennas trailing behind.
It circled Earth about once every 96 minutes, sending simple radio beeps that amateur listeners could pick up.
People around the world tuned in. In the United States, the news caused real alarm.
The next year, the US launched its first satellite and created NASA. The space race had begun.
Sputnik’s batteries ran out after about three weeks. In early 1958 it fell back and burned up.
It weighed about 84 kilograms. Which space first would you have wanted to watch live?
Before railways, every British town kept its own time.
visual: Period photo of a town clock (public domain)

voiceover: Towns set their clocks by the sun. Noon was when the sun was highest over that town.
So a western town like Bristol ran about ten minutes behind London, every single day.
visual: Map: London and Bristol with clocks

voiceover: That was fine for horses. But trains moved fast, and timetables with different local times caused confusion.
In the 1840s, railway companies began using London time, also called railway time, across their networks.
visual: Map: rail lines with matching clocks

voiceover: Some towns showed both times for years. A few clocks even had two minute hands. Bristol’s Corn Exchange clock still does.
visual: Simple graphic: clock with two minute hands

voiceover: In 1880, a law made Greenwich Mean Time the legal time across Great Britain.
How would you plan a trip if every town kept its own time?
A whole Roman legion vanishes from the records.
visual: Museum open-access photo of a Roman inscription

voiceover: The Ninth Legion, about five thousand soldiers, served in Roman Britain and helped found the fortress at York.
visual: Map of Roman Britain, pin on York

voiceover: An inscription in York, from around AD 108, is the last firm record of it in Britain.
After that, it is missing from later lists of legions. So what happened to it?
The popular story says it marched into Scotland and was destroyed. A famous 1954 novel spread that version.
visual: Re-creation: map of Scotland with question mark

voiceover: But no Roman source records that defeat. Some finds suggest parts of it later served near the Rhine.
visual: Map: Britain to the Rhine arrow

voiceover: Historians still debate whether it was lost in a war in the east or disbanded.
visual: Timeline graphic: possible endings with question marks

voiceover: Which theory do you think fits the evidence best?
In 218 BC, elephants marched over the Alps.
visual: Period painting of the Alps crossing (public domain)

voiceover: Hannibal was a general from Carthage, in North Africa, at war with Rome.
Instead of attacking by sea, he marched from Spain, across southern Gaul and over the mountains.
visual: Map: route from Spain to Italy

voiceover: He brought war elephants, reportedly about 37 of them, along with tens of thousands of soldiers.
The crossing happened in autumn, with snow, narrow paths and steep drops. Many men and animals were lost.
Ancient writers describe the march, but nobody agrees which pass he used. Several are proposed.
visual: Map: several possible passes with question marks

voiceover: He reached Italy and won major battles there, but Rome won the war in the end.
It remains one of history’s most famous marches. Which ancient journey do you think was the hardest?
Magna Carta failed within weeks. It became famous anyway.
visual: Public-domain image of a Magna Carta manuscript

voiceover: In June 1215, rebel barons forced King John to agree to a charter at Runnymede, near London.
It promised that the king would follow the law, and limited unfair taxes and seizures.
The popular version says it gave rights to everyone. In fact it mostly protected barons and free men.
visual: Simple graphic: small group highlighted in a crowd

voiceover: John asked the Pope to cancel it. Within about ten weeks it was annulled, and war followed.
After John died, it was reissued several times, and later versions entered English law.
Only a few of its clauses are still law in England today, but its ideas spread far.
Which old document do you think still matters most?
For a century, maps showed California as an island.
visual: Public-domain map with California as an island

voiceover: Early Spanish explorers had mapped it correctly in the 1500s, as a long peninsula.
visual: Old map showing a peninsula (public domain)

voiceover: Then in the early 1600s, island maps appeared. One possible source was a misread or exaggerated expedition report.
Mapmakers in Europe copied each other. Once one famous map showed an island, many more followed.
visual: Re-creation: maps copied in a chain

voiceover: Few people in Europe could check. Most mapmakers never travelled to the places they drew.
visual: Simple graphic: mapmaker at a desk, ocean between

voiceover: Overland trips by missionaries around 1700 showed that California was joined to the mainland.
visual: Map: overland route around the gulf

voiceover: Even so, island maps kept appearing for decades, until a Spanish decree in 1747 declared California not an island.
Old maps can be wrong for a long time. Which old map mistake do you find funniest?
Canned food existed for decades before the can opener.
visual: Period illustration of early tin cans (public domain)

voiceover: In the 1790s, France needed a better way to feed its army and navy on long campaigns.
A confectioner named Nicolas Appert sealed cooked food in glass jars and heated them. The food kept for months.
visual: Re-creation: glass jars in boiling water

voiceover: Nobody yet knew why it worked. Germs weren’t understood until Louis Pasteur’s work decades later.
In 1810, a British patent covered sealing food in tin-plated iron cans, which were tougher than glass.
Early cans were thick and heavy. Users reportedly opened them with tools like hammers and chisels.
visual: Re-creation: hammer and chisel beside a can

voiceover: Dedicated can openers only appeared around the 1850s, once cans became thinner.
Which other invention do you think came in the wrong order?
